newsitem.title: USA: Clinton praises Bosnians, reaffirms U.S. commitment.
newsitem.headline: Clinton praises Bosnians, reaffirms U.S. commitment.

text.p: President Bill Clinton praised Bosnians on Sunday for their relatively peaceful election, but said the job of building democracy was not finished and the United States would do its part to help.
Clinton told reporters at the White House the road ahead would be "hard" but that the Bosnian people had taken a "remarkable step forward."

He said the United States would maintain its commitments in the region, but did not specifically address the role of U.S. troops or the politically sensitive issue of their scheduled withdrawal by Dec. 20, a year after their current mission started.

"By voting yesterday the Bosnian people gave life to the institutions of national government -- the presidency, the parliament, the constitutional court and key government agencies," Clinton said. "These institutions can bring the country together instead of driving it apart."
He acknowledged that new challenges lay ahead to get the government "up and running" to build a "unified democratic and peaceful Bosnia."

"Our commitment to Bosnia does not end with these elections," Clinton said. "We will continue to do our part to hold Bosnia's leaders to their commitments and to turn the promise of more than nine months ago in Dayton into a reality," he said referring to the Bosnia peace agreement reached in Dayton, Ohio, last November.

In coming months, the United States and its allies will have to decide what, if any, peacekeeping force will remain in Bosnia. Some believe that once the NATO peacekeepers pull out, fighting between the Muslims, Serbs and Croats could resume.

Madeleine Albright, the U.S. ambassador to the United Nations, said on Sunday it was "premature" to say whether U.S. troops might remain on the ground in Bosnia after the current U.N. peacekeeping mission ends in December.
"We do not believe that there will be any necessity for a security function," she said on NBC's "Meet the Press."
"There will be a necessity for economic assistance at that point and also humanitarian assistance. So it is premature to talk about what a post-IFOR (U.N. implementation force) would look like."
